summary: Describes SRL, a language for writing rulesets, which are configuration files loaded into a traffic flow meter. The rules say which flows to measure and what information to store for each. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a rule book written for a counting machine, telling it what to watch and what to write down.

questions: what is srl traffic flow language
how to write rulesets for a traffic flow meter
what does the srl count statement do
subtitle: A simple procedural language for writing rulesets that tell a traffic flow meter what to measure.

tldr.problem: Rulesets for an RTFM traffic flow meter were machine code for its Packet Matching Engine, which users found confusing and difficult to write.
tldr.mechanism: SRL is a procedural language with IF, SAVE, COUNT, subroutines and similar statements. SRL programs are compiled into rulesets that can be downloaded to meters.
tldr.outcome: Users can write effective rulesets without understanding the engine's details. An SRL compiler was available in NeTraMet version 4.2.

today: RFC 2723 is an Informational memo from October 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A ruleset for an RTFM meter is a sequence of instructions for the meter's Packet Matching Engine (PME). The RFC says most users find these instructions confusing and hard to write, because each instruction's effect depends on the engine's state when it runs.

SRL, the Simple Ruleset Language, is a procedural language for creating such rulesets. Programs are compiled and downloaded to meters. An SRL compiler is part of NeTraMet, a free-software implementation of the RTFM meter and manager, version 4.2. The language may also suit other applications that select traffic flows from a stream of packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The counting machine only understands a tricky code. SRL lets people write the instructions in plain, readable steps instead.

sections.title: RTFM Meters and Flows
sections.content:
An RTFM traffic flow is a stream of packets seen by a meter between two end points, or to and from a single end point. Each end point is described by address attributes such as PeerType, PeerAddress, TransType and TransAddress. For IPv4 traffic, PeerType is 1, TransType is TCP (6), UDP (17) or ICMP (1), and TransAddress is usually a port number.

Flows are bi-directional: each flow record has one set of counters for packets from source to destination and another for returning packets. A ruleset specifies which flows to measure and which attributes to store. A meter may run multiple rulesets, with every packet processed by each.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is like a conversation between two people. The meter keeps two tallies: what each person said to the other.

sections.title: How an SRL Program Runs
sections.content:
An SRL program runs from the beginning for each new packet. It has two goals: decide whether the packet is part of a flow of interest and, if needed, which end is the source; then SAVE the attributes that identify the flow and COUNT its quantities.

The engine first uses source and destination as they appear on the wire. If they do not match a flow to record, it normally runs the program again with source and destination swapped. This is how one record gets forward and backward counters. A programmer can suppress the reverse matching if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: For every packet the machine reads the rules top to bottom. If it does not fit, it flips the sender and receiver and tries once more.

sections.title: Language Elements
sections.content:
Comments start with a hash sign, statements usually end with a semicolon, identifiers start with a letter, and case is not significant. DEFINE name = text; gives simple parameterless text substitution.

An IF statement tests an attribute against an operand list with ==, combined with && and ||. Each operand is a value with an optional mask or width, so 130.216/16 and 130.216.0.0 & 255.255.0.0 are equivalent. An ELSE always matches the immediately preceding IF. Compound statements in braces can be labelled and left with EXIT.

  • SAVE records what identifies the flow but writes nothing to the table.
  • COUNT builds the flow identifier from saved attributes, finds or creates the table entry and increments its counters.
  • IGNORE drops the packet; NOMATCH says matching failed, causing the swapped retry or, if already swapped, an ignore.
  • STORE assigns to one of six variables (SourceClass, DestClass, FlowClass, SourceKind, DestKind, FlowKind), reset to zero for each packet.

Subroutines are declared with SUBROUTINE ... ENDSUB, take ADDRESS or VARIABLE parameters, and are called with CALL ... ENDCALL. The caller supplies numbered statements, and RETURN n jumps to the one labelled n:.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book has simple moves: look at the packet, write down who it is, and add one to the tally. You can also skip it, or flip it around.

sections.title: Example Programs
sections.content:
The first example classifies IP port numbers. It defines names for IPv4, protocols and the well-known ports, ignores packets that are not IPv4, and uses NOMATCH so that the well-known port ends up as the destination. It saves the transport type, both 32-bit peer addresses, and a FlowKind of 'W' for www, 'F' for ftp, 'T' for telnet or '?' for anything else.

The second classifies traffic into groups of networks. A subroutine net_kind checks whether an address is in the user's own network or in a list of other networks, saves the network part at 16 or 24 bits, stores 10, 20 or 30, and returns to label 1, 2 or 3. The network numbers sit in two DEFINEs so they are easy to change.
sections.plainLanguage: One example sorts packets by what kind of website or service they use. The other sorts them by which neighborhood they come from.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC says SRL, being a language for configuration files, presents no security issues in itself. However, flow data gathered with such rulesets may be valuable, so access to the meter and its data should be secured as discussed in the RTFM Architecture and Meter MIB documents.

For IANA, the RFC points to Appendix C, which lists the RTFM attributes by name and their value sizes in bytes. Because SRL refers to attributes by name, users do not need attribute numbers. Allocating new attributes is covered in the RTFM Architecture document.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book is harmless, but the numbers the machine collects can be private, so the machine should be kept locked.
